ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a cube, and three intersecting faces can be seen: the top face is labeled 14, the front face is labeled 15, and the right face is labeled 11. These three visible faces all meet along edges, so they are pairwise adjacent, and no two of them are opposite faces. Reasoning: The numbers on the six faces are consecutive integers, and the sums of the two numbers on each of the three pairs of opposite faces are all equal. Since the visible numbers include 11, 14, 15, the six consecutive integers can only be 10,11,12,13,14,15 or 11,12,13,14,15,16. If they are 10 to 15, the total sum is 75, and the sum of each opposite pair should be 25, so the pairings can only be (10,15), (11,14), (12,13), which would make 11 and 14 opposite; but in the figure, the faces with 11 and 14 are adjacent, a contradiction. Therefore it can only be 11 to 16. Their sum is 11+12+13+14+15+16=81.

method.method_draft: Read the cube image first: the three visible faces are labeled 14 on top, 15 on the front, and 11 on the right; since these faces meet at edges, they are pairwise adjacent, so none of these three visible numbers are opposite each other. From the text, the six face numbers are consecutive whole numbers and each opposite-face pair has the same sum. Test the possible blocks of six consecutive integers containing the visible extremes 11 and 15: they can only be 10–15 or 11–16. For 10–15, the only equal-sum opposite pairings would be (10,15), (11,14), and (12,13), forcing 11 and 14 to be opposite, which contradicts the image because the right and top faces are adjacent. Therefore the block must be 11–16. Sum these six numbers: 11+12+13+14+15+16 = 81.
